content:
Mathlib does not have basic numerical analysis theorems. For example, the forward Euler method is not defined. In https://github.com/Vilin97/forward_euler I defined it and proved that it converges to the true solution as the time step shrinks. I used a strong assumption that the RHS of the ODE is globally bounded -- it can be relaxed with some extra work but I first want to understand if there is interest in this kind of work.

I split the formalization into two PRs. One has nothing to do with the Euler method, and is just about regular grids and linear interpolation. The second PR is about the forward Euler method specifically.

For transparency, this is my first time making heavy use of Claude Code for a mathlib PR. The initial version of the formalization was done by Aristotle, and then I went through many (20+) iterations of factoring out lemmas, golfing, simplifying proofs using Claude Code. I do believe that the final code is reasonably high quality -- probably higher than if I was writing it myself. The initial formalization took Aristotle 2 hours, and I spent ~12 hours iterating on it with Claude Code.

Are people reluctant to look at PRs that were submitted with Claude's help? Is this a red flag in the community? Or do people think that numerical analysis is unimportant / does not belong in mathlib? Or are the PRs too large?
I am in the dark here, trying to understand why the PRs are not being considered.
People have many things that demand their time
Just to give you some data, I have 3 open PRs without help of AI I patently waited for more than a month. This is not about AI or specific topics. It is the average review speed here

I see. I must have gotten lucky with my previous PRs.

  1. Is there anything that a contributor can do to make it easier/faster to get their PRs reviewed?
  2. It feels like it would be useful to have a Mathlib Reviewer Agent that can catch many common issues like code style, naming, insufficient generality, etc. That would probably give the reviewers more time to focus on actual deep reviews. In fact, Copilot can already make reviews, but it lacks mathlib-specific conventions (example). Are there reasons against having such an agent?

Vasily Ilin said:

  1. It feels like it would be useful to have a Mathlib Reviewer Agent that can catch many common issues like code style, naming, insufficient generality, etc.

This is what linters are for, which run in CI. See #mathlib4 > linter requests for active work in adding more linters.

Specifically, there are already linters for code style, and naming linters in PRs. For generality, there are linters that check your use of typeclasses (both existing and planned), and there used to be a linter for "you don't need [Ring R] here, just [Semiring R]" and the like but I'm not sure if someone is working on it anymore.

Do you have concrete suggestions for such things that an LLM would be much better at than a deterministic script? A few people triggered Copilot reviews on their PRs and the results look pretty bad to me. There's also a Mathlib-specific LLM reviewer #general > botbaki which you can trigger by writing @botbaki review on your PR.

Vasily Ilin said:

Are people reluctant to look at PRs that were submitted with Claude's help? Is this a red flag in the community?

I will note that in general, PR descriptions that look AI-generated make me reluctant to look at a PR. They're usually an annoying wall of text that indicate to me that the author did not take manual care when opening the PR. This does not necessarily apply to your PRs, just my personal "red flags".
Specifically for your PRs, my personal suggestion is to remove the titles ("Summary" and "Motivation"). Also trim the summary on the first PR, I don't see the value in repeating the names of lemmas from the diff if there's nothing to add about them. The summary of the second PR seems nicer.

Let me add that currently, (a) raw LLM output is very far from mathlib's standards, and (b) too many contributors use LLMs to formalise something and think that's it (i.e., being oblivious that the cleaning up just starts then), and (c) the number of such PRs (or zulip posts to a personal repo) has increased a lot recently. This makes me hesitant to review LLM-written PRs in general. The fact that we all have a lot to do doesn't help.
All of these apply to AI PRs in general, not necessarily to yours --- but it means you should try to communicate clearly that your PR is not one of the "slop" ones.

To give you some indicate what reviewers are looking for, https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/pr-review.html helps. In particular, skimming your PR for 30 seconds, I wonder whether

  • all these lemmas should be in this file, or some can find a better home,
  • most of your linear interpolation file should be generalised to not just regular grids.

(In general, "what is the natural generality for my lemma" is a key question to ask yourself. Be prepared for reviewers asking you this one, and for generalising your lemmas as necessary.)

I have addressed all the suggestions on the PR.
The following is intended as a genuine question, not criticism:

How long should I wait before pinging individual people for the review? I see that Patrick Massot was assigned as a reviewer, should I ping them after a week or two of no review?
I will never review any LLM-written code.

Let me clarify that we're seeing an uptick in LLM-generated contributions, who sometimes even use LLMs to respond to reviewer messages. That's the antithesis of valuing (the already very scarce) reviewer time. Any sign of that is a good way to make your PRs not looked at.

Positively speaking: show the reviewers that you care. That you understand all the Lean code and all design decisions made there. That you carefully inspected the code and cleaned it up to your best ability --- before making a PR. Read the PR review guide and try to follow it! When a reviewer points out a problem once, fix it in other locations also, etc.

While I understand a sentiment "Generalising my lemmas made them 100 lines longer, so I disagree with them", be aware that mathlib style is different: we optimise for building the overall library, so generalising a lemma makes it useful elsewhere, we'd generalise it, every time.
As Andrew Yang put it: optimise the size of your PR, minus the lemmas that should be in mathlib already.

Thank you for your advice, Michael!

Would it not be more productive to cure poison with poison and make an LLM reviewer that can uphold all the rules of mathlib PRs? Speaking more practically, I did clean up the code to the best of my ability before the PR: commit history here). And happy to clean it up further for the PR. I want mathlib to have numerical analysis!

I used conventions.md on https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/35753/changes/fc0363654ca3679fcacd4ab0f130b4bc82eabfd7. I don't actually know if these are good suggestions. Can anyone validate?

  1. Rule 103 — Avoid @[simp] lemmas with hard side conditions. piecewiseLinear_apply_grid is @[simp], but requires StrictMono x as a hypothesis. simp will almost never discharge that, so the tag probably is not earning its keep. Candidate: drop @[simp].

  2. Rule 17 / Rule 198 — Standard case-split / structured destructuring idioms. In continuous_piecewiseLinear,
    rcases eq_or_lt_of_le ht.2 with rfl | h_lt
    could be
    obtain rfl | h_lt := eq_or_lt_of_le ht.2
    for consistency with the obtains elsewhere in the file.

  3. Rule 19 — Shape goals explicitly with show / change.
    refine (show ContinuousOn _ _ from by fun_prop).congr ?_
    is a somewhat awkward show … from by … sandwich. It could be rewritten as
    refine (by fun_prop : ContinuousOn (fun t => …) _).congr ?_
    or split into a named have.

  4. Rule 53 / Rule 210 — Prefer direct contradiction tools (by_contra!, contrapose!). In gridIdx_mem_Ico, both
    lt_of_not_ge fun h => …
    and
    not_lt.mp fun hlt => not_lt.mpr hn …
    could read more directly with by_contra!.

  5. Rule 297 — Prefer ≤ / < over ≥ / >. lt_of_not_ge in gridIdx_mem_Ico could likely be rephrased to use ≤ / <.

  6. Rule 244 — Prefer let over set unless you need the defining equation.
    set n := gridIdx x t in hasDerivWithinAt_piecewiseLinear: here the substitution in h1, h2 is used, so set is probably correct, but worth confirming.

  7. Rule 393 — Add comments to long, delicate, or non-obvious proofs. hasDerivWithinAt_piecewiseLinear is a dense pipe-chain; a one-line comment on what .congr_of_eventuallyEq and .congr_deriv are doing could help future readers.

  8. Rule 5 — Prefer clear proof structure over golfing. Meta-check after the golf pass: gridIdx_mem_Ico’s BddAbove inline term with
    not_lt.mp fun hlt => not_lt.mpr hn …
    is dense and might be worth expanding back into a short tactic block.

  9. Rule 321 / Rule 325 — Casing / variant suffixes. continuous_piecewiseLinear_ofValues mixes piecewiseLinear (camel case) with ofValues (camel case) inside a snake_case theorem name. Debatable whether _ofValues should be _of_values; mathlib has precedent for both.

  10. Rule 400 — Add characteristic lemmas for new definitions. gridIdx has two characteristic lemmas (_eq_of_mem_Ico, _mem_Ico); piecewiseLinear has _eq_on_Ico and _apply_grid. That is probably sufficient, but worth confirming that nothing else obvious is missing, such as a gridIdx lemma at t = x n specifically.

@Vasily Ilin Most of these are pretty easy to figure out yourself just by looking at existing Mathlib code, using your own judgement, or asking Claude for deeper analysis:

(1) is obviously correct if you have a general understanding of what simp is doing. The @[simp] tag is for automating obvious simplifications and rewriting goals into a normalized form--not for theorems that require additional hypotheses.

(6) is similar, you just need to know the difference between let and set (the former just makes a definition, the latter makes a substitution). Claude already explained that set was likely necessary here because you are using the substitution. If you want to double-check, you can just change let to set in the code and see if it breaks the proof.

(3) & (4) are stylistic choices for proofs. You should just try rewriting the proofs with the suggested changes and determine for yourself if it improves the proof or not.

(7) & (8) are about comments. There is no hard and fast rule for this. You should use your own judgement in determining if the comments are necessary to make the proof readable.

(2) and (5) are about standard conventions. I asked Claude: "Does Mathlib have a strong preference for ≤ / < or ≥ / >?" and "Does mathlib have a preference for rcases or obtain" I asked it to go through various folders and use grep to determine which was more common. It determined that there was a very strong preference for le over ge, likely due to the fact that this helps with unification in rw/simp tactics. It determined that rcases or obtain are both used frequently, but there was a slight preference for obtain especially in newer code.

(9) is already documented in https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/naming.html -- see rule 5 in particular for explaining this convention.

(10) is not really a suggestion, just a general hint that something might be missing from your API. You can usually just prompt "Can you think of any reusable API lemmas that would be nice to add for gridIdx?" and see if it comes up with anything.

Vasily Ilin said:

The hope is that we can help new contributors like myself and AI write better mathlib-style code -- saving reviewers' time. I don't know how to validate this list of rules except by using it on real PRs and seeing if the feedback is actually helpful.

I am all for saving reviewers' time, but I am not sure this is the best way to accomplish that. IMO you are responsible for auditing the output of your LLM. Copy/pasting "here's ten things Claude said I should do... what do you think?" offloads that responsibility onto reviewers. If you can not understand what Claude is talking about, you can ask it to elaborate on it's suggestions, or you can ask specific questions on Zulip about what you don't understand.

For what it's worth, I have tried your conventions.md and I did not really notice a difference in output quality. The main issue is that there are too many rules, so Claude can not actually analyze all of them in a single turn. Many are too specific to be widely applicable or are too vague to be useful. A few contradict each other. In the end, Claude ends up picking a random scattershot of rules, and applies them more-or-less arbitrarily. The improvements are usually positive, but I can get similar results just by prompting "How can I clean up this code?" or "Does this conform to the Mathlib standards?" or "Compare my API to [similar file in Mathlib] and tell me how to make it more idiomatic."

I think a more effective approach than conventions.md would be to write a standardized agentic workflow for taking unoptimized LLM code and refactoring it into something that's reasonably close to the standards of a Mathlib PR. Something like:

  1. Organize sections, defs, files into a coherent project structure.
  2. Check that theorems/definitions are mathematically coherent.
  3. Check all theorems/definitions are stated with minimum assumptions / maximum generality.
  4. Check for instance diamonds, @[simp] tags, large imports, performance bottlenecks
  5. Search for repeated patterns/arguments and pull them into auxiliary lemmas.
  6. Golf proofs. Avoid unstable patterns like non-terminal simp.
  7. Add boilerplate API. Implement all expected instances.
  8. Cross-verify against linters, style guide, naming guide, similar files in Mathlib.
  9. Edit docstrings. Add bibliography, copyright and author attributions
  10. Log changes. Git commit. Split off into smaller branches/PRs as necessary.

Ideally, each of these steps would have it's own instructions.md with concise, meaningful advice on how to best optimize for that one aspect of Mathlib. You'd run the whole process many times in a loop, with a top-level agents managing subordinates—all aggressively critiquing each others' work until the whole system steadily converges to a local minimum.

Let me add: the main point of reviewing is about teaching PR authors. If you try to understand if a comment made elsewhere applies, that's fair - but then show us you tried to understand. Where are you at; what do you understand, what are you unsure about? Show us you want to learn.
With my moderator head on: let's keep discussions about prompting AIs to #Prompting, skills, and agent tools
